name: 2 Kings

overview.author: Not stated. Jewish tradition credits Jeremiah. It continues 1 Kings and draws on royal annals.
overview.date: The events cover about 853–561 BC. The book was completed during the exile, after Jehoiachin’s release in 561 BC (25:27).
overview.audience: The exiles in Babylon, asking why God’s people had lost the land, the temple, and the throne.
overview.setting: The northern kingdom of Israel until its fall to Assyria in 722 BC, and the southern kingdom of Judah until Jerusalem’s fall to Babylon in 586 BC.
overview.purpose: To show that exile came because both kingdoms persistently rejected God’s word through the prophets, while God remained patient, preserved a remnant, and kept a lamp burning for David’s line.
overview.structure: Elisha’s ministry and the divided kingdoms (1–17), ending with Israel’s fall, then Judah alone (18–25), from Hezekiah and Josiah’s reforms to Babylon’s destruction of Jerusalem.

outline.title: The Divided Kingdom to Israel’s Fall

themes.title: God’s Patience
themes.text: God sends prophet after prophet to warn His people before judgment falls (17:13–14).

themes.title: The Power of God’s Word
themes.text: Prophetic words come true precisely, both in blessing and judgment.

themes.title: Idolatry Leads to Exile
themes.text: Both kingdoms fall because they worship other gods and refuse to listen.

themes.title: Faith in Crisis
themes.text: Hezekiah spreads Assyria’s threatening letter before the LORD and sees deliverance.

themes.title: Reform and Its Limits
themes.text: Josiah’s wholehearted reform cannot undo generations of sin; a deeper renewal is needed.

themes.title: Hope for David’s Line
themes.text: The book ends with the Davidic king released from prison, a small sign that God’s promise lives.

christInBook.text: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves and has some left over, foreshadowing Jesus feeding the multitudes.
Naaman, a Gentile leper, is cleansed by humble faith (Luke 4:27).
Elisha raising the Shunammite’s son anticipates Jesus’ power over death.
The release of David’s heir hints at the coming King who will sit on David’s throne forever (Luke 1:32–33).

reflection: Elisha asked for a double portion of God’s Spirit. What do you most want God to do in and through you?
Elisha’s servant saw only the enemy army until his eyes were opened (6:17). What spiritual realities do you need eyes to see?
Naaman nearly missed healing because of pride (5:11–12). Where is pride keeping you from simple obedience?
Hezekiah spread his trouble before the LORD (19:14). What do you need to lay out before God?
Josiah responded to God’s word with tears and action. How do you respond when Scripture convicts you?

chapterList.title: Elijah and Ahaziah
chapterList.summary: Injured King Ahaziah of Israel sends messengers to ask Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, if he will recover. Elijah intercepts them: “Is it because there is no God in Israel?” Fire consumes two companies of soldiers sent to seize Elijah, but the humble third captain is spared. Ahaziah dies.
questions: Why was consulting Baal-zebub so offensive to God?
What made the third captain different?
Where are you tempted to seek help apart from God?

chapterList.title: Elijah Taken Up; Elisha Succeeds Him
chapterList.summary: Elisha refuses to leave Elijah and asks for a double portion of his spirit. A chariot of fire appears, and Elijah goes up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha takes Elijah’s cloak, strikes the Jordan, and it parts. He heals Jericho’s water.
questions: What does Elisha’s persistence (2:2, 4, 6) teach?
What does the “double portion” mean (see Deuteronomy 21:17)?
How does Elijah’s departure compare with Jesus’ ascension (Acts 1:9–11)?

chapterList.title: Victory over Moab
chapterList.summary: Israel, Judah, and Edom march against Moab and run out of water. Elisha, for Jehoshaphat’s sake, prophesies that God will fill the valley with water without wind or rain. Moab sees the water red in the sun, thinks it is blood, and is defeated.
questions: Why does Elisha help only for Jehoshaphat’s sake?
What does it mean to “dig ditches” in faith, preparing for God’s provision?
How does God use what seems natural to accomplish His purpose?

chapterList.title: Elisha’s Miracles of Provision
chapterList.summary: Elisha multiplies a widow’s oil to pay her debt. A Shunammite woman provides him a room, and God gives her a son. When the boy dies, Elisha raises him. Elisha makes poisoned stew harmless and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves.
questions: How does the widow’s oil flow as long as she has jars?
What does the Shunammite woman’s faith look like (4:26)?
How does Jesus’ feeding of the 5,000 echo 4:42–44?

chapterList.title: Naaman Healed
chapterList.summary: Naaman, a Syrian commander, has leprosy. An Israelite servant girl tells him about Elisha. Elisha tells him to wash in the Jordan seven times, and he angrily almost refuses, but humbles himself and is healed. Naaman confesses the God of Israel. Gehazi greedily takes gifts and is struck with leprosy.
questions: What role does the little servant girl play?
Why was it hard for Naaman to obey such a simple command?
What lesson does Gehazi’s greed teach?

chapterList.title: The Floating Axe Head; Chariots of Fire
chapterList.summary: Elisha makes a borrowed axe head float. When the Syrian army surrounds Dothan, Elisha prays that his servant’s eyes be opened, and he sees horses and chariots of fire. The Syrian army is blinded, then fed and released. Later, Samaria endures a terrible famine under siege.
questions: What does the axe head story say about God’s care for small things?
Pray Elisha’s prayer (6:17) for yourself. What would you need to see?
Why did Elisha feed his enemies (6:22–23)?

chapterList.title: The Siege Lifted
chapterList.summary: Elisha prophesies that food will be cheap by tomorrow. Four lepers find the Syrian camp deserted, because God made the Syrians hear a great army. “This day is a day of good news,” they say, and they share it. The doubting officer sees it but does not eat.
questions: What does the lepers’ realization in 7:9 teach about sharing good news?
Why was the officer punished?
How does this story picture the gospel?

chapterList.title: The Shunammite’s Land; Hazael; Kings of Judah
chapterList.summary: The Shunammite woman’s land is restored. Elisha weeps as he foresees the evil Hazael will do to Israel, and Hazael murders Ben-hadad to become king. Jehoram and Ahaziah reign in Judah, following Ahab’s ways, yet God will not destroy Judah for David’s sake.
questions: How is God’s timing evident in the restoration of the woman’s land?
Why did Elisha weep (8:11–12)?
What does 8:19 reveal about God’s covenant faithfulness?

chapterList.title: Jehu Anointed King
chapterList.summary: A prophet anoints Jehu king over Israel to destroy Ahab’s house. Jehu drives furiously and kills King Joram of Israel and King Ahaziah of Judah. Jezebel is thrown from a window and eaten by dogs, as Elijah foretold.
questions: How is Elijah’s prophecy about Jezebel fulfilled?
What does Jehu’s zeal accomplish, and what are its limits?
How does God bring justice in His time?

chapterList.title: Jehu Destroys Ahab’s House and Baal Worship
chapterList.summary: Jehu kills Ahab’s 70 sons and Baal’s prophets and destroys Baal’s temple. But he does not turn from Jeroboam’s golden calves or walk in God’s law with all his heart.
questions: What did Jehu do well?
What did Jehu fail to do (10:29–31)?
How can zeal against others’ sins coexist with blindness to our own?

chapterList.title: Athaliah and Joash
chapterList.summary: Athaliah, Ahab’s daughter, seizes Judah’s throne and kills the royal heirs, but baby Joash is hidden in the temple for six years. The priest Jehoiada crowns Joash, Athaliah is executed, and the people renew their covenant with God.
questions: How does God preserve David’s line when it is almost wiped out?
What role does Jehosheba’s courage play?
How does this foreshadow Herod’s attempt on baby Jesus (Matthew 2)?

chapterList.title: Joash Repairs the Temple
chapterList.summary: Joash does right while Jehoiada instructs him. He collects money to repair the temple, using a chest for offerings. But later, he gives temple treasures to Syria’s King Hazael, and his servants assassinate him.
questions: Why did Joash do right only “all his days... because Jehoiada instructed him” (12:2)?
What do you learn from the honest workmen (12:15)?
How can our faith become our own and not only borrowed?

chapterList.title: Jehoahaz, Jehoash, and Elisha’s Death
chapterList.summary: God has compassion on Israel and relieves them from Syria. Dying Elisha tells King Jehoash to strike the ground with arrows; he strikes only three times, limiting his victories. A dead man thrown into Elisha’s grave comes back to life.
questions: What does 13:23 reveal about God’s compassion?
What does the king’s half-hearted striking teach?
What does the miracle at Elisha’s grave suggest?

chapterList.title: Amaziah and Jeroboam II
chapterList.summary: Amaziah of Judah does right but not like David. After defeating Edom, he foolishly challenges Israel and is defeated. In Israel, Jeroboam II restores borders, as Jonah prophesied, because God saw Israel’s bitter affliction.
questions: How did success lead Amaziah into pride?
Why did God help Israel under wicked Jeroboam II (14:26–27)?
Who is the prophet mentioned in 14:25?

chapterList.title: Kings of Judah and Israel
chapterList.summary: Azariah (Uzziah) and Jotham reign in Judah fairly well. Israel’s kings rapidly assassinate one another. Assyria’s King Tiglath-pileser begins taking Israelite territory and people.
questions: What pattern of violence marks Israel’s last kings?
What does Uzziah’s leprosy indicate (see 2 Chronicles 26:16–21)?
How do unstable times reveal spiritual decline?

chapterList.title: Ahaz of Judah
chapterList.summary: Ahaz walks in the ways of Israel’s kings, even burning his son as an offering. Threatened by Syria and Israel, he asks Assyria for help and copies a pagan altar for the temple.
questions: Why did Ahaz turn to Assyria instead of God (see Isaiah 7)?
What does copying the pagan altar say about his heart?
Where are you tempted to rely on worldly power for security?

chapterList.title: The Fall of Israel
chapterList.summary: Assyria captures Samaria in 722 BC and exiles Israel. The writer explains why: they feared other gods, rejected God’s statutes, ignored the prophets, and became false. Foreign peoples are settled in Samaria, mixing worship of the LORD with their own gods.
questions: List the reasons given for Israel’s fall (17:7–23).
How did God warn them (17:13)?
What does it mean to “fear the LORD but also serve their own gods” (17:33)?

chapterList.title: Hezekiah and Assyria’s Threat
chapterList.summary: Hezekiah trusts the LORD like no king before him and destroys idols, even the bronze serpent. Assyria’s King Sennacherib invades Judah, and his official mocks Hezekiah’s trust in God before Jerusalem’s walls.
questions: Why did Hezekiah destroy the bronze serpent (18:4)?
What is the Rabshakeh’s strategy in his speech?
How does the enemy try to undermine our trust in God today?

chapterList.title: Hezekiah’s Prayer and Jerusalem’s Deliverance
chapterList.summary: Hezekiah spreads Sennacherib’s threatening letter before the LORD and prays. Isaiah prophesies that Assyria will not enter the city. That night the angel of the LORD strikes 185,000 Assyrians, and Sennacherib is later killed by his sons.
questions: What can you learn from Hezekiah’s prayer (19:15–19)?
What is the ultimate purpose of the deliverance (19:19)?
What “letter” do you need to spread before the LORD?

chapterList.title: Hezekiah’s Illness and Pride
chapterList.summary: Hezekiah is told he will die, prays tearfully, and God adds fifteen years, giving a sign of the shadow moving backward. But he proudly shows Babylonian envoys all his treasures, and Isaiah prophesies that everything will be carried to Babylon.
questions: How does God respond to Hezekiah’s tears?
Why was showing his treasures to Babylon so foolish?
What does Hezekiah’s response in 20:19 reveal?

chapterList.title: Manasseh and Amon
chapterList.summary: Manasseh, Hezekiah’s son, reigns 55 years and does more evil than the Canaanites: idols in the temple, child sacrifice, sorcery, and shedding much innocent blood. God declares that He will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish. Amon follows his father’s evil.
questions: How could Hezekiah’s son become so wicked?
What does 2 Chronicles 33:10–16 add about Manasseh?
How do the sins of one generation affect the next?

chapterList.title: Josiah Finds the Book of the Law
chapterList.summary: Young King Josiah repairs the temple, and the high priest finds the Book of the Law. When Josiah hears it, he tears his clothes. The prophetess Huldah says judgment will come, but not in Josiah’s day, because his heart was tender and he humbled himself.
questions: How could God’s word be “lost” in His own temple?
What does Josiah’s response teach about how to receive Scripture?
How does God honor a tender heart (22:19)?

chapterList.title: Josiah’s Reforms
chapterList.summary: Josiah reads the law to all the people, renews the covenant, destroys idols and pagan shrines throughout the land (fulfilling a prophecy from 1 Kings 13), and celebrates a great Passover. No king turned to the LORD like him, yet God’s anger against Judah remains. Josiah dies in battle.
questions: What did Josiah’s reform involve?
How was 1 Kings 13:2 fulfilled?
Why did judgment still come (23:26)?

chapterList.title: Babylon Invades Judah
chapterList.summary: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon subjugates Judah. King Jehoiakim rebels, and raiders attack Judah “according to the word of the LORD.” Jehoiachin surrenders, and Babylon carries off the temple treasures and 10,000 captives, including Ezekiel. Zedekiah is made king.
questions: Why did these disasters come (24:3–4)?
How does Daniel 1:1–2 connect to this chapter?
How do Jeremiah’s letters (Jeremiah 29) speak to these exiles?

chapterList.title: The Fall of Jerusalem
chapterList.summary: Zedekiah rebels, and Babylon besieges Jerusalem. The city falls in 586 BC; Zedekiah’s sons are killed before his eyes, and he is blinded. The temple, palace, and houses are burned, and the people are exiled. Years later, Jehoiachin is released from prison and eats at the king of Babylon’s table.
questions: How does the end of Kings fulfill God’s warnings (Deuteronomy 28)?
Why might the book end with Jehoiachin’s release?
Where do you find hope in seasons of loss?

tagline: The long decline to exile, and God’s patient prophets
readingPlan: 25 chapters: one chapter a day takes 25 days; two a day takes about 13 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
